summary: Genitourinary cancers are large markets that are changing fast. In early bladder cancer, a wave of therapies delivered directly into the bladder aims to spare patients bladder removal and repeat surgeries. In prostate cancer, PSMA-targeted drugs and T cell engagers are moving from late-stage disease toward earlier treatment.

sections.heading: Bladder cancer basics
sections.body: About three-quarters of new bladder cancers are non-muscle-invasive (NMIBC): confined to the bladder lining. Standard care is surgical removal through the urethra (TURBT), followed for higher-risk disease by BCG, a weakened bacterium instilled into the bladder to provoke an immune response. When BCG stops working (BCG-unresponsive), the traditional option is removing the bladder (cystectomy), a major operation that many patients want to avoid. Lower-risk tumors often come back again and again, meaning repeated surgeries.

sections.heading: New bladder therapies
sections.body: Most new treatments are intravesical, placed directly into the bladder through a catheter. They include gene therapies, oncolytic viruses, an IL-15 immune stimulant and slow-release drug devices and gels. In BCG-unresponsive disease, regulators accept single-arm trials measuring the complete response rate, so how long responses last (for example at 12 months) is the key way to compare products.

sections.heading: Prostate cancer
sections.body: Localized prostate cancer is treated with surgery or radiation, often combined with hormone therapy, and new drugs aim to lower the chance of recurrence. Metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer (mCRPC) keeps growing despite hormone therapy. Many tumors display PSMA, the target of radioligand therapy (Pluvicto) and of experimental T cell engagers that link T cells to cancer cells. Masked engagers switch on only inside tumors, to reduce side effects.

sections.heading: What investors watch
sections.body:
• Complete response rate and 12-month durability in bladder cancer.
  • Ease of use in urology clinics: storage, handling and treatment schedule.
  • Disease-free survival in localized prostate cancer, and PSA and imaging responses in mCRPC.
  • Crowding: several approved and late-stage options now compete for the same patients.
